Redundancy

Modular Organization and Hierarchical Structure

Modules exhibit hierarchical organization across  5-7 octaves of temporal scales: from millisecond cerebellar predictions to multi-year schemas in ventromedial PFC

Enables parallel processing; some theories of modularity, such as Fodor’s, propose that certain modules operate with a degree of "informational encapsulation," meaning they can perform their specific computations without extensive reference to other psychological systems, further enhancing processing speed for dedicated tasks; this further leads to extensibility (evolvability; no need for complete redesign, just modular extension and broad scaling) and robustness (damage to one specialized module may not necessarily lead to a catastrophic failure of the entire system)

Each level of hierarchy shows characteristic timescale ratio of  5-7× relative to adjacent levels, suggesting fundamental engineering regularities

Ascending the hierarchy roughly corresponds to increasing the timescale of representation learning, increasing inference-time representational stability? 1, and the potential for top-down influence

Types of invariance

Spatial: translation, rotation, scale

Temporal: speed, phase

Categorical: within-class variation

Context: background, lighting

Functional connectivity among networks is dynamic and context-dependent. Modularity enables flexible reconfiguration of processing networks based on task demands, allowing the same anatomical substrate to support diverse world modeling contexts through dynamic connectivity changes

Two visual streams, one spatial and one semantic

Anterior-posterior processing gradients organize temporal abstraction, with posterior regions processing immediate sensory information and anterior regions handling extended temporal contexts and future-oriented prediction. This principle is evident in sensory pathways that ascend from primary cortices to higher-order association areas, and also within specific cortical regions. For instance, the lateral prefrontal cortex (LPFC) exhibits a functional hierarchy where caudal (posterior) areas are more involved with concrete, present-oriented information and task details, while rostral (anterior) areas handle more abstract, future-oriented information and overarching goals. This ascent in the processing hierarchy often corresponds to an increase in the timescale of representation learning and an enhancement in the stability of representations during inference

Types of abstraction

Prototype/Entity Extraction

Statistical centers of categories

Stored in anterior temporal lobe

Rapid generalization to new instances

Coexists with exemplar memories

Relational Abstraction

Relations independent of specific entities

Prefrontal and parietal substrates

Enables analogical reasoning

Structured like language

Specific brain regions or neuronal populations are highly specialized for representing particular types of information (e.g., fusiform face area for faces, parahippocampal place area for scenes)

Small-World Organization and Efficiency

Human brain networks exhibit small-world topology: high local clustering (0.4-0.6) combined with short average path lengths ( 3 steps between any two regions), enabling efficient information transfer at minimal wiring cost. This optimizes the trade-off between local processing efficiency and global integration capacity, enabling rapid information transmission while maintaining modular specialization for different aspects of world modeling

This architecture achieves  35% reduction in wiring length compared to random networks while maintaining similar communication efficiency.

Small-worldness (σ = clustering/path-length ratio) typically ranges 1.5-3.0 in healthy brains, declining with aging and neurological disorders

Rich-Club Organization and Network Hubs: top 15-20% of highly connected regions form a "rich-club" backbone consuming  80% of the brain’s communication capacity

Hub nodes link networks, modalities, conceptual subspaces, timescales, and cognitive domains; hubs are essential for complex cognitive functions that necessitate drawing upon and synthesizing information from multiple, often disparate, sources. For example, constructing a unified episodic memory of an event requires binding together visual, auditory, spatial, emotional, and conceptual information, a process heavily reliant on hub regions like the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. The structural connectivity provided by white matter pathways forms the anatomical backbone that enables this functional integration across the brain. Convergence zones and integrative hubs, such as the anterior temporal lobe (ATL) for semantic memory, exemplify this principle, bringing together information from various modality-specific areas to form supramodal concepts.

Energetic and Spatial Constraints

Brain consumes  20% of body’s energy despite being  2% of body weight

Wiring minimization principle:  60-70% of connections are to spatially adjacent regions

Across mammalian cortex the probability (or weight) of a cortico-cortical projection falls off roughly exponentially with Euclidean distance. Tracer data show a decay length of λ 5-10mm for macaque inter-areal links and an even steeper fall-off for microscopic intracortical axons. Simulations using this single-parameter rule reproduce rich-club hubs, small-world efficiency and overall wire-length minimisation. 2, 3

Recent work proves that for any system optimizing relevance versus compression, power laws emerge automatically in the frequency distributions of optimal representations, suggesting that neural connectivity patterns encoding these representations would also exhibit power-law distributions. 4

Lognormal weight rule - synaptic strengths and inter-areal weights span 4-5 orders of magnitude and are well fit by a lognormal distribution, producing a "skeleton of strong links in a sea of weak ones." 5

Trade-off between minimizing wiring cost and maximizing topological efficiency drives modular organization

Structural wiring and myelination follow an economy-efficiency trade-off: long-range axons consume ∼60% of the brain’s metabolic budget yet occupy only  5% of volume, enforcing sparse high-bandwidth highways atop dense local recurrence.

Hemispheric Specialization and Integration

Hemispheric specialization emerges from the minimization of wiring costs and the need for parallel processing

Interhemispheric connections via corpus callosum ( 200 million axons) predominantly link homotopic regions

Left hemisphere shows denser local connectivity for language regions; right hemisphere shows longer-range connectivity for spatial attention

Callosal connections show specific developmental timing critical for establishing lateralized functions

Network Robustness and Degeneracy

Multiple overlapping pathways between any two regions provide robustness to damage

Cognitive functions map to distributed networks rather than single regions - lesion of any single node rarely eliminates function completely

Developmental plasticity allows alternative network configurations to support similar functions (degeneracy principle)
